title: Fort Massapeag — Public Historical Marker
summary: Public signs at Sunset Park introduce Massapequa history, Native–Dutch diplomacy and the preservation of Fort Massapeag. A new interpretive sign was unveiled in April 2026.
address_label: Public historical sign near Fairfax Road and Gloucester Road, Sunset Park, Massapequa, NY
map_geometry_source: OpenStreetMap tourism=information node 13135135699, via Mapcarta: public sign at 40.65313, -73.46121; cross-checked with Town of Oyster Bay’s Fairfax / Gloucester marker location, September 12, 2026.
why_this_matters: Fort Massapeag brings Native diplomacy and exchange into a suburban landscape where that history can be easy to overlook. Its public signs also show how historical interpretation changes as researchers reconsider old stories and communities choose what to remember.
introduction_title: Massapequa history in the public landscape
introduction_content:
The public historical signs near Fairfax and Gloucester Roads introduce Fort Massapeag, a place connected with Massapequa life and colonial trade. The Town of Oyster Bay lists the roadside marker in its historic places guide.[7]

Begin with Tackapousha, the Massapequa sachem who represented his people in a March 1656 peace agreement with Dutch director-general Peter Stuyvesant.[6]
history_content:
A fort remembered in land records

A deed dated July 13, 1696 refers to an old fort at Fort Neck. Archaeological evidence later led researchers to interpret Massapeag as a place of Native–Dutch exchange, including possible wampum production. A Dutch-directed fortified trading post dating to 1656 is an interpretation of the evidence, rather than a surviving construction record.[6]

1993: national recognition

Fort Massapeag became a National Historic Landmark in 1993, recognizing the importance of its archaeological record.[6]

April 2026: a new public sign

The Town of Oyster Bay unveiled a new interpretive sign on Fairfax Road in April 2026, bringing the fort’s history to people passing through the neighborhood.[8]

Older accounts associated Fort Neck with a 1653 battle led by John Underhill. The town’s historic places guide notes that this tradition is disputed; the story should not be treated as a settled account of what happened at this fort.[7]
preservation_title: Read the signs; protect the place
preservation_content:
Use the public signs and established park routes to learn about this history. Leave the ground, plants and any objects undisturbed.

View Oscar Hefting’s photograph of the National Historic Landmark sign. This image documents the landmark sign, distinct from the interpretation unveiled in 2026. Read the report on the 2026 sign.

Continue with Massapequa history and Tackapausha Museum and Preserve.
whereintheworld_title: Begin at the public historical sign
whereintheworld_content: The pin marks the public information sign near Fairfax Road and Gloucester Road at Sunset Park in Massapequa. The Town of Oyster Bay’s guide identifies this street intersection as the marker location.[7]
